subtopic: Catching someone else in a lie
passage:
Indu found her calculator in the front pocket of Aditi's school bag on Thursday, while looking for a pen Aditi had said she could borrow. The same calculator Aditi had "definitely returned" two weeks ago.
The hostel dorm was full. Three girls were at the next bunk. Indu could have held it up and said, "Look what I found."
She didn't. After study hour she asked Aditi to walk with her to the water cooler.
"I found my calculator in your bag. You told me you'd given it back."
Aditi's face crumpled. "I was going to. I dropped it and the screen got a line. I was scared you'd be angry."
"Why did lying feel easier than telling me?"
"Because you'd look at me like I'm careless."
"I'd be annoyed about the screen. I'm more upset about the lie. You're not a bad person, Aditi. It was a bad choice."
Aditi nodded, wiping her eyes. "I'll pay for the screen."

qa.q: Where did Indu find the calculator?
qa.a: Indu found it in the front pocket of Aditi's school bag.

qa.q: Why did Aditi lie about returning the calculator?
qa.a: Aditi was scared Indu would be angry and see her as careless after the screen got a line, so lying felt easier than telling the truth.

qa.q: What did Indu do that made the confrontation work?
qa.a: Indu spoke privately instead of in the full dorm, named what she knew, asked why lying felt easier, and separated Aditi from the bad choice.

qa.q: What would change if Indu had held the calculator up in the dorm?
qa.a: Aditi would have been shamed in front of three other girls, making her more likely to deny it or hide things in future.

grounding: Indu finds that Aditi lied and confronts her privately, naming what she knows, asking why, and separating the person from the act.

subtopic: Catching someone else in a lie
passage:
Dear Sharmila,
I'm writing because I don't trust myself to say this calmly out loud yet, and I want to get it right.
On Saturday you said you were studying at Mehul's house. I saw your location on the family app later: you were at the lake with a group until ten. I know that much.
I'll be honest, my first plan was to ask you, very innocently, "How was Mehul's?" and watch you lie again. I decided not to. That would be a trap, and traps just teach people to hide better.
So here's what I want to ask instead: why did it feel safer to lie than to ask me? Is it something about how I react?
Lying was a wrong choice. It doesn't make you a bad daughter. I love you exactly as much as I did on Friday.
Can we talk tonight after dinner, just us?
Papa
Pranav

qa.q: Until what time was Sharmila at the lake?
qa.a: Sharmila was at the lake with a group until ten.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling that led to writing instead of talking?
qa.a: Pranav was hurt and upset, not yet sure of staying calm out loud, but wanted to handle it carefully.

qa.q: Which choice in the letter protects the relationship best?
qa.a: Pranav refuses to trap Sharmila, names only what is known, asks why lying felt safer, and separates Sharmila from the wrong choice.

qa.q: How might Sharmila feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Sharmila might feel ashamed but also relieved that Papa is not shaming or trapping and is asking to talk, which could make telling the truth easier.

grounding: Pranav, signing as Papa, finds that Sharmila lied, names what is known, refuses to trap or shame, and asks why lying felt necessary.

subtopic: Catching someone else in a lie
passage:
Sonali, can we talk here, just us, not in the group? It's me, Sudha, not the class monitor, okay?
I know you weren't sick on Saturday. I saw your story from the mall with your cousins. I'm not going to post it or tell anyone. I just want to say what I know, straight, instead of pretending I don't.
I'm not angry at you as a person. You're still my best friend. I'm upset about the lie, because I waited at the library for two hours and I was worried about you.
So can I ask why it felt like you had to lie? Did you think I'd be upset that you went with them? Because honestly, I might have been a bit jealous. But I'd rather know.
You don't have to answer right now. I'm going to get us two cutting chais. When I come back, you can tell me, or not.

qa.q: How long did Sudha wait at the library?
qa.a: Two hours.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling about the lie?
qa.a: Sudha felt upset and a bit jealous after waiting and worrying for two hours, but not angry at Sonali as a person.

qa.q: Which parts of Sudha's approach avoid humiliating Sonali?
qa.a: Talking privately, not posting or telling anyone, saying plainly what is known, separating the friend from the lie, and asking why it felt necessary.

qa.q: What might it be like for Sonali to hear this?
qa.a: Sonali may feel caught and embarrassed but also relieved, since Sonali isn't shamed in front of the group and is given time to explain.

grounding: Shows a teenager confronting a friend's lie privately, naming what is known and asking why, while separating the friend from the act.

subtopic: Catching someone else in a lie
passage:
I was doing homework at the dining table, so I heard all of it, even though Papa pulled the door halfway shut.
Deepika didi had said she was studying at Rupali's house on Saturday night. Papa had phoned Rupali's mother about something else and found out didi wasn't there.
I thought he'd shout. He didn't. He sat on the edge of her bed and said, "I know you weren't at Rupali's. Aunty told me. I'm not going to trick you by asking where you were."
Didi went red and said nothing.
Then he said, "I love you. The lie is what I'm upset about, not you. I want to understand why it felt like you couldn't tell me."
After a long time didi said something I couldn't hear and started crying. Papa passed her the tissue box.
He never mentioned it at dinner in front of us. I don't know exactly what she said. But she's been telling him where she goes since then.

qa.q: How did Papa find out Deepika didi wasn't at Rupali's?
qa.a: Papa had phoned Rupali's mother about something else and found out.

qa.q: What might Deepika didi have been feeling when Papa sat on her bed?
qa.a: Deepika didi went red and silent, likely ashamed and scared, before crying once she felt understood.

qa.q: Which choices made Papa's confrontation work?
qa.a: He said plainly what he knew instead of setting a trap, separated his love for her from the lie, asked why it felt necessary, and never raised it in front of others.

qa.q: What would change if Papa had asked 'Where were you?' to catch her out?
qa.a: Deepika didi might have lied again to escape, making the hiding worse instead of opening a real conversation.

grounding: Shows, through a younger sibling's eyes, a father confronting a teenager's lie without traps or public shaming, naming what he knows and asking why.

subtopic: Catching someone else in a lie
passage:
Monday: Ishita found her missing maths notebook in Indu's bag during PE, her own name scribbled out on the cover. Her first thought was to hold it up in front of the whole class. She didn't. She put it back and went home furious.
Wednesday: After school, by the cycle stand, she said quietly, "Indu, I saw my notebook in your bag on Monday. I know you took it. I'm not going to tell the class. But why? You could have just asked to copy."
Indu stared at her shoes. "I've failed two tests. My parents are paying for extra tuition and I still failed. I was too ashamed to ask."
The following Monday: Indu gave the notebook back with a note: "Sorry. I shouldn't have taken it." At lunch Ishita showed her how she had solved the quadratic ones. They sat together till the bell.

qa.q: Where did Ishita find her notebook?
qa.a: In Indu's bag during PE, her own name scribbled out on the cover.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel on Monday, and what did she want to do?
qa.a: Ishita was furious and wanted to hold the notebook up in front of the whole class, but chose not to.

qa.q: What did Ishita do on Wednesday that helped Indu tell the truth?
qa.a: She spoke privately, named exactly what she saw, promised not to tell the class, and asked why Indu felt she had to take it.

qa.q: Why did Indu take the notebook instead of asking?
qa.a: Indu was ashamed after failing two tests despite extra tuition, and asking to copy felt too embarrassing.

grounding: Shows a teenager who catches a classmate's lie choosing a private, calm question over public shaming, and the truth coming out.

subtopic: Catching someone else in a lie
passage:
Ritu, you asked why I didn't shout at your cousin yesterday. Sit, and let your Nani Gurleen tell you about Harleen.

We were fifteen, in the same class in Moga, practising a play for the school function. One Sunday Harleen told me she had fever and couldn't come. That evening my brother saw her at the mela, laughing on the swings.

The other girls wanted me to ask her in front of everyone on Monday, so she would squirm. I nearly did. Instead I waited by the canal after school and said, "I know you were at the mela. I'm not angry about the swings. Why did you feel you had to lie to me?"

She cried then. Her father had forbidden the play, and she was too ashamed to say so.

I told her, "You're still my friend. The lie was a bad choice, not a bad you."

We found her a backstage job her father allowed, and she never lied to me again.

qa.q: Where did Gurleen wait to talk to Harleen?
qa.a: Gurleen waited by the canal after school.

qa.q: What was Gurleen tempted to do at first, and why might she have felt that way?
qa.a: She felt hurt at being lied to by a close friend and nearly let the other girls make Harleen squirm in front of everyone.

qa.q: Which choice by Gurleen at fifteen turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Taking Harleen aside by the canal, saying what she knew and asking why, instead of a public confrontation; it left room for the truth and kept the friendship.

qa.q: What was it like for Harleen when Gurleen asked 'why' instead of accusing her?
qa.a: Harleen felt safe enough to cry and share the real reason, her father's ban on the play, because she wasn't being trapped or mocked.

grounding: Illustrates confronting a friend's lie privately: naming what is known, asking why it felt necessary, and separating the person from the act instead of shaming her.
